title_content.content: Fedspeak divided but point to a near-term hold

paragraph_content.content: Comments from policymakers this week suggest most officials are comfortable holding rates steady in the near term.

Chair Warsh did not comment on the near-term policy outlook in his first Humphrey Hawkins testimony, but his remarks highlighted his dovish bias. Chair Warsh reiterated that AI should be disinflationary over the medium term and argued that AI-related capex would generate only a one-time price shock. He continued to highlight optimism about supply-side expansion and its impact on inflation. Warsh also stepped back from relying on the trimmed-mean inflation measure and suggested that the Fed's data task force would consider alternative measures, including private sector price data.

Warsh reiterated his preference for a smaller balance sheet. He continued to hint that this might lead to an easier rate policy. He argued that officials should monitor monetary aggregates and suggested that money supply measures might have helped identify inflation risks in 2021. Warsh further argued that balance sheet decisions should remain an FOMC policy matter and be communicated “well in advance,” rather than treated as a technical function delegated to the NY Fed.

Other policymakers, such as NY Fed President Williams, Governor Cook, and Vice Chair Jefferson, appeared comfortable with a wait-and-see approach. Speaking before the June CPI report, Governor Waller seemed to be cautious about inflation risks, and mentioned that policy decisions should be based on incoming inflation data. We think the June CPI and PPI reports are likely to convince him to remain on hold at the July meeting. Most centrist officials appear comfortable remaining on hold as they expect sequential disinflation going ahead.

By contrast, several officials remained hawkish. Dallas Fed President Logan argued that AI-related demand is “already here” and adding to inflationary pressure. KC Fed President Schmid said his focus “remains on inflation in setting the correct course of policy,” while Cleveland Fed President Hammack saw no conflict between the Fed’s mandates and argued that further action may be needed to curb inflation.

Regarding future work by the task forces, Fedspeak suggested some disagreement among the FOMC participants. Waller proposed some modifications to the dot plot, but saw the median dot as a useful benchmark to discuss policy stance. Schmid argued that releasing economic outlook is a good communication practice. Also, Schmid called for an inclusion of food components into core inflation, while Warsh indicated that the task force on data sources would discuss how to gauge the inflation trend.
Growth data continued to point to resilient economic activity. Retail sales rose
m-o-m in June, while prior months were revised higher. Excluding gasoline, spending remained firm, and based on our estimate of the retail deflator, real retail sales rose
m-o-m, lifting the three-month average to its strongest pace since April 2025.

The July Beige Book painted a similar picture, with consumer spending remaining resilient. Notably, there were fewer references to divergence between high- and low-income households than in previous reports. Overall, the data suggest consumption has remained robust despite headwinds from the Iran conflict. We have revised up our Q2 GDP tracking estimate to 2.9% q-o-q ar from 2.3% last week. Our estimate for real final sales to private domestic purchasers stands at 3.4%, up from 2.9% previously.
We expect the pace of new home sales rose in June, while survey data likely pointed to robust activity in July.

Jobless claims (Thursday): Both initial and continuing claims fell this week. Overall, claims data have trended lower and remained subdued lately, pointing to few layoffs and a resilient labor market.

S&P PMIs (Friday): The preliminary print of the S&P manufacturing PMI likely picked up in July. Regional surveys released thus far suggest activity in the manufacturing sector has continued to expand at a solid pace, and demand indicators have improved. Price indices likely remained elevated.

The preliminary print of the S&P services PMI likely remained in expansionary territory. The NY Fed services survey for July pointed to a rebound in activity. We expect the employment index returned to expansionary territory, in line with other surveys.

New home sales (Friday): We expect the pace of new home sales edged up to 600k in June from 580k in May. New home sales fell sharply in the last two months, likely due to headwinds from Iran war-related uncertainty and elevated mortgage rates. We expect some of this negative impact reversed in June.

paragraph_content.content: We expect the Fed to stay on hold indefinitely (with risks skewed towards hikes) due to persistent price pressures, stable labor markets and waning political pressure.

Economic activity: Growth has remained robust lately, supported by easing tariff uncertainty, fiscal stimulus from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the lagged impact of Fed rate cuts amid easy financial conditions. Business investment appears to be broadening beyond the AI sector. Despite higher energy prices stemming from the Iran war, consumption has held up, partly due to higher tax refunds and strong payroll income growth. NFPs have been volatile, but an array of indicators point to stabilization and tentative signs of reacceleration in the labor market. While the recent decline in the unemployment rate was due to a one-off factor, we expect the unemployment rate to eventually edge lower to

by year-end. The US economy remains relatively insulated from the crude oil price shock due to the Iran war, owing to the small share of energy-goods consumption in household spending, as well as domestic energy production.
Inflation: Core inflation remains well above the Fed's
target, and risks appear skewed to the upside. We forecast Q4 2026 core PCE inflation of
y-o-y, but the BEA's planned methodological changes to certain PCE price components could reduce core PCE inflation by about 20bp to

y-o-y in Q4 2026. Wage growth is moderating and tariff-related price pressures are abating, but new AI-related price pressures from robust demand and supply shortages could push up goods inflation. Overall, we expect core PCE inflation to peak in coming months on lower oil prices, residual seasonality and moderating wage growth. We expect rent disinflation to continue, albeit gradually.

Policy: We expect the Fed to remain on hold indefinitely. Fed Chair Warsh likely remains motivated to ease, but recent elevated inflation readings and hawkish Fedspeak suggest he may not be able to convince the majority to support cuts. In addition, he is likely to encourage the committee to keep policy rates steady until recently announced task forces make recommendations on different aspects of data and monetary policy. While near-term hikes appear unlikely, the Fed's hesitance to respond to tentative signs of inflation pressure raises the risk that it may end up "behind the curve" and need to hike quickly to re-establish credibility. The balance of risks tilts towards tightening. On tariffs, wider Section 122 exemptions, lower tariff rates and a focus on affordability suggest limited further escalation of US trade policy. We don't expect substantial economic stimulus from another reconciliation by Republicans before mid-terms.

Risks: Further escalation of geopolitical risks could lead to a tightening of financial conditions and a worsening of the fiscal outlook. Increased political pressures on FOMC participants could undermine the Fed's credibility and cause sharp market reactions. An AI bust could lead to material corrections in asset valuations and reduced business investment. A continued shortage of memory chips and supply-chain disruptions due to a protracted Iran war could lead to a second round
